the impact of neighborhood resources on coronary heart disease and ischemic stroke.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

living in a neighborhood with a high proportion of fast food restaurants, bars/pubs and health care facilities is associated with a modestly increased risk of coronary heart diseases and stroke, but this association may be due to unmeasured confounding.
neighborhood deprivation, rather than availability of neighborhood resources per se, may contribute to the risk of cardiovascular disease.
the neighborhood is a small, but still important, contributor to the risk of cardiovascular disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neighborhood is a complex environment with both positive and negative influences on the health of the residents.
neighborhood deprivation is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, which is mediated by neighborhood resources and individual lifestyle.
living in a deprived neighborhood is associated both with a high risk of lifestyle risk factors as well as a high risk of cardiovascular disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neighborhood environment is not a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
the risk of cardiovascular disease varies with the neighborhood-level deprivation, which is an important finding for the planning of future public health strategies.
it is important to consider the neighborhood context when investigating the impact of neighborhood resources on health.
